summary: Lists questions authors should be prepared to answer for any IPv6 multihoming solution. The questions do not assume multihoming is the only problem. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a quiz that anyone proposing a new multi-road internet connection idea should be able to pass before others believe it.

questions: what questions should multihoming solutions answer
subtitle: A checklist of questions for IPv6 multihoming solution designers.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a solution for multihoming—allowing sites to connect through multiple providers—but proposed solutions vary widely in approach and impact, making it hard to evaluate which trades off risks appropriately.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4219 provides a comprehensive questionnaire organized around six areas: on-the-wire behavior, identifiers and locators, routing interactions, DNS interactions, application compatibility, and security concerns. Solution designers must answer these questions.
tldr.outcome: The questionnaire helps solution designers identify gaps in their proposals and helps the community understand the practical consequences of different design choices, enabling informed decisions about which tradeoffs to accept.

today: RFC 4219 is an Informational RFC that provides a systematic questionnaire for evaluating IPv6 multihoming solutions. While IPv6 multihoming solutions have evolved since 2005, the underlying design questions remain relevant for assessing how solutions impact network operations, routing, applications, and security.

sections.title: The Multihoming Challenge
sections.content:
At the time RFC 4219 was written, multiple proposed solutions to IPv6 multihoming existed, each with different architectural approaches. The document does not propose a specific solution; instead, it defines practical operational questions that any solution must address.

The RFC presumes familiarity with RFC 3582, which covers the high-level requirements for IPv6 multihoming. The goal is to ensure that solutions do not introduce more problems than they solve, particularly for both single-homed and multihomed deployments.
sections.eli5: Different teams proposed different ways to solve multihoming. Before picking a winner, engineers need to check whether the solution creates new problems as bad as what it fixes.

sections.title: Protocol and Identifier Design
sections.content:
Solutions must explain how they solve multihoming, at which network layer they operate, and why that layer is appropriate. Each layer has tradeoffs: transport-layer solutions require changes to every transport protocol, while IP-layer solutions may require packet expansion or changes to the pseudo-header, affecting transport implementations.

The questionnaire also explores whether solutions separate identifiers (stable names for communication endpoints) from locators (network addresses that might change). Key questions include whether the solution adds packet overhead or latency, how identifier-to-locator bindings update when paths become available or unavailable, how hosts learn and manage multiple identifiers, and how bindings are authenticated. Solutions must also clarify whether they address mobility, handle fragmentation, and interact with existing protocols like Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: Does the solution make packets bigger or slower? If it splits addresses into names and locations, how do machines keep the bindings straight when paths change? Can it work with existing mobile protocols?

sections.title: Routing, DNS, and Internet Integration
sections.content:
The RFC examines how multihoming solutions affect the Internet's routing system and DNS. Solutions must address whether they change route aggregation—today's internet scales because prefixes are aggregated into relatively few routing table entries. Solutions must also explain whether they enable traffic engineering, allow sites to manage traffic flows, and whether new namespaces require aggregation.

Since DNS is central to internet operation, solutions must explain their relationship to DNS and any new identifier namespaces, including how mappings are defined and what new DNS zones or record types might be needed. The questionnaire addresses interactions with split-view DNS, centralized registration requirements, DNS circular dependencies, multihomed DNS servers, DNS server load implications, upstream provider requirements, and debugging tools needed. Solutions must also consider interactions with Autonomous System numbering, changes to ICMP error handling, and whether aggregation at provider boundaries prevents sites from controlling traffic.
sections.eli5: Does the solution make routers' tables explode? Can site operators control their traffic? Does it break DNS or create circular dependencies? What happens if the DNS server itself is multihomed?

sections.title: Applications and Deployment
sections.content:
Solutions must identify what API and application changes are required. Will legacy applications using gethostbyname() or getaddrinfo() work unchanged? What happens when applications log IP addresses or expect them to be meaningful?

The RFC asks whether solutions are incrementally deployable alongside existing IPv6 and whether multihoming is mandatory or optional. Further questions address IPv4 backward compatibility, impact on different site types (single-homed, small multihomed, large multihomed, ad-hoc, and short-lived wireless), middlebox interactions, handling of referrals in protocols like FTP and peer-to-peer systems, and impacts on real complex applications like SIP and RTSP.
sections.eli5: Will old programs keep working? What about people using simple IPv6? Do wireless networks need special handling? Does the solution break common apps like voice calls?

sections.title: Security and Legal Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC asks how secure a multihoming solution should be, with the principle that the worst case should be no worse than current IPv6. Solutions must consider whether they open hosts to time-based attacks, what threat analysis has been done, and whether they introduce auditing or privacy concerns—since IP addresses are often tied to individuals.

Legal considerations address whether solutions introduce new mnemonics or namespaces involving trademarks, and what organizations might be required to manage new name spaces. The questionnaire emphasizes that comprehensive threat analysis is essential and references RFC 4218 (Threats Relating to IPv6 Multihoming Solutions) for more details.
sections.eli5: Does the solution create new ways to attack machines or steal privacy? Is it at least as secure as today's internet? Does it involve trademark concerns?
